claims.text: Untreated, pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin native oxide film.
At room temperature, the native oxide film remains compact.
At room temperature, the native oxide film acts as a barrier to chloride ions and oxygen.
The native oxide provides notable corrosion protection to Q235 steel in a chloride-rich environment at room temperature.
Exposure at approximately 60–80°C compromises the integrity of the native oxide film relative to exposure at approximately 25°C.
Elevated-temperature degradation of the native oxide may involve increased porosity or oxide phase changes.
Loss of native-oxide integrity permits easier penetration of chloride ions and oxygen.
Increased penetration of chloride ions and oxygen promotes localized galvanic cells.
Localized galvanic activity leads to localized corrosion, including pitting, and accelerates overall corrosion.
Elevated-temperature samples will exhibit earlier onset of localized corrosion than room-temperature samples.
Elevated-temperature samples will exhibit greater pit density than room-temperature samples.
Elevated-temperature samples will exhibit a higher overall corrosion rate than room-temperature samples.
Elevated-temperature samples will show detectable changes in native-oxide morphology and composition relative to room-temperature samples.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply when temperature is the only varied factor and may not apply when mechanical stress, other reactive species, or alloy modifications are significant.
The temperature threshold and kinetics for the proposed oxide transformation have not been precisely quantified.
